items.stem: A 72-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has a 2-year history of short-stepped shuffling gait, with relatively preserved arm swing, normal tremor examination, and no response to levodopa. MRI shows extensive periventricular and subcortical white matter infarcts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Vascular parkinsonism produces predominant lower body signs, a magnetic gait, little tremor, and poor levodopa response in a patient with risk factors and extensive small vessel disease or strategic infarcts on imaging. Idiopathic disease features asymmetric upper limb tremor with clear levodopa response. Multiple system atrophy brings early autonomic failure, and progressive supranuclear palsy brings vertical gaze palsy and early falls.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has progressive dystonia, dysarthria, and a pigmentary retinopathy. MRI shows bilateral low signal in the globus pallidus with a central bright spot. Which gene is most likely involved?
items.explanation: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, produces dystonia, parkinsonism, and retinopathy with the eye of the tiger sign, a central hyperintensity within a hypointense globus pallidus. Wilson disease shows copper accumulation with different imaging and Kayser-Fleischer rings, TOR1A dystonia has normal imaging, and Huntington disease shows caudate atrophy. Genetic confirmation is by sequencing, and iron chelation has not been shown to alter the course reliably.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has 1 year of involuntary forceful eyelid closure that makes reading and driving unsafe. Eye examination is normal. Which is the preferred initial treatment?
options: Systemic corticosteroids for 6 weeks with slow taper
items.explanation: Blepharospasm is a focal dystonia of the orbicularis oculi, and botulinum toxin injections give benefit in most patients, repeated every few months. Oral agents are less effective and often poorly tolerated. Corticosteroids and immunoglobulin treat inflammatory disease, which is not present, and surgical closure of the lids would not treat the dystonia and risks functional blindness.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent develops a twisting posture of the right foot that progresses over 2 years to involve the trunk and arms. Brain MRI is normal. Which gene is most likely involved?
items.explanation: Early-onset generalized torsion dystonia with limb onset, normal imaging, and normal cognition is typical of the GAG deletion in TOR1A, an autosomal dominant disorder with reduced penetrance. GCH1 causes dopa-responsive dystonia with diurnal variation, PANK2 causes a neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation and MRI changes, and ATP7B causes Wilson disease. Pallidal deep brain stimulation helps patients refractory to medication.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has foot dystonia and parkinsonism beginning at age 24. Her symptoms improve markedly with low-dose levodopa, and her brother is similarly affected while her parents are healthy. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Young-onset parkinsonism with an excellent levodopa response, early foot dystonia, and affected siblings of unaffected parents suggests autosomal recessive disease, most often due to PRKN mutations. SNCA mutations and duplications and LRRK2 mutations are autosomal dominant and usually produce later onset. MAPT mutations cause frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism rather than a levodopa-responsive juvenile syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by sequencing and dosage analysis, and early-onset disease raises motor complication risk.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 12 years and now has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and choreiform finger movements. He is clinically stable on his antipsychotic. Which is the most appropriate treatment for the movements?
items.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia follows prolonged exposure to dopamine receptor blockers, and VMAT2 inhibitors are the drugs with evidence from randomized trials. Anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia, and raising the antipsychotic dose may mask but ultimately aggravate it. Levodopa has no benefit. Switching to a lower-risk agent such as clozapine can also be considered with psychiatry.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman whose mother has Huntington disease asks about predictive testing. She is asymptomatic and has not yet decided about children. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Order the test immediately through primary care without any counseling
Refuse testing because it is never allowed
Structured pretest counseling before any genetic testing
items.explanation: Predictive testing for Huntington disease is offered to at-risk adults after structured counseling covering psychological readiness, support, insurance and employment concerns, and reproductive options, because no disease-modifying treatment exists. Testing minors for an adult-onset condition is discouraged. A blanket refusal is not appropriate for a competent adult, and testing without counseling can cause harm. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis and prenatal options can be discussed as part of the counseling process.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a 2-year history of progressive ataxia, dysarthria, urinary urgency, and a fall in standing blood pressure. Family history is negative, and genetic panels for spinocerebellar ataxias are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Sporadic adult-onset ataxia with early autonomic failure fits the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy, where autonomic failure helps separate it from idiopathic late-onset cerebellar ataxia. Friedreich ataxia begins in youth with areflexia and cardiomyopathy, and dominant spinocerebellar ataxias have a family history and positive genetic tests. Drug-related atrophy would not explain progressive dysautonomia in this setting.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has an action tremor of both hands for 8 years without rest tremor or bradykinesia. His mother and uncle have similar tremor. Examination shows normal tone and arm swing. Which statement best distinguishes his condition from Parkinson disease?
options: The tremor shows pill-rolling at rest
The tremor appears with posture and action, not mainly at rest
He has hyposmia and REM sleep behavior disorder that precede symptoms
items.explanation: Essential tremor is an action tremor, usually bilateral and symmetric, often with family history, and lacks the bradykinesia and rigidity of Parkinson disease. Rest tremor with pill rolling, hyposmia, and REM sleep behavior disorder all point to Parkinson disease. Because bradykinesia is absent here, levodopa would not be indicated. The tremor may improve temporarily with beta-blockers, which supports essential tremor rather than parkinsonism.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has backward falls within 2 years of symptom onset, axial rigidity, a startled stare, and difficulty looking down while reflexes are brisk. Levodopa gave no benefit. Which pathology is most likely?
options: A four-repeat tauopathy involving the midbrain and basal ganglia
Alpha-synuclein inclusions within oligodendroglial cells and neurons
Prion protein deposition in the cortex
items.explanation: Early falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, and axial rigidity define Richardson syndrome of progressive supranuclear palsy, a four-repeat tauopathy. Glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein characterize multiple system atrophy. TDP-43 is the substrate in many cases of frontotemporal dementia and ALS, and prion deposition causes rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus. Neuropathology shows globose neurofibrillary tangles and tufted astrocytes, which distinguishes it from the synuclein disorders at autopsy.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has progressive leg dystonia and toe walking that is mild in the morning and worsens through the day. Symptoms improve dramatically after sleep. Which treatment is both diagnostic and therapeutic?
options: Botulinum toxin to the calf muscles
items.explanation: Dopa-responsive dystonia, most often from autosomal dominant GCH1 mutations, presents in childhood with diurnal fluctuation and a sustained, dramatic response to small doses of levodopa. Any child with unexplained dystonia deserves a levodopa trial. Anticholinergics and baclofen are options for other dystonias and botulinum toxin treats focal symptoms, but none reverses this disorder. Sustained benefit without early motor complications is characteristic, and confirmation can be made by genetic testing or biopterin studies.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with diabetes develops sudden violent flinging movements of the right arm and leg. MRI shows a small acute infarct. Where is the lesion most likely located?
items.explanation: Hemiballismus results from damage to the subthalamic nucleus, most often by a small vascular lesion, and produces contralateral large amplitude flinging of the proximal limbs. The side of the lesion is opposite the movements. A caudate lesion may cause chorea or behavioral change, and a cerebellar lesion causes ipsilateral ataxia. Treatment is with dopamine blockers or VMAT2 inhibitors, and it often resolves spontaneously.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has progressive ataxia, conjunctival telangiectasias, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and choreoathetosis. Which laboratory finding is typical?
options: Elevated very long chain fatty acids
items.explanation: Ataxia telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder due to ATM mutations, with cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, and increased malignancy risk and radiation sensitivity. Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated and immunoglobulins such as IgA are often reduced. Low ceruloplasmin suggests Wilson disease, and the other tests point to different conditions. Radiation exposure should be minimized because of chromosomal instability, and surveillance for lymphoma and leukemia is needed.

items.stem: A 66-year-old retired teacher has a 14-month history of a right hand rest tremor, slowed handwriting, and reduced arm swing. Examination shows asymmetric cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia with a normal gait base. Which treatment gives the greatest symptomatic benefit for motor features?
options: Pramipexole at the maximum tolerated dose
items.explanation: Levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic therapy for the motor features of Parkinson disease and is the reference standard against which other agents are measured. Dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors give milder benefit, which is why they are used for mild disease or as adjuncts. Trihexyphenidyl helps tremor in some younger patients but does little for bradykinesia and carries cognitive risk in older adults.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has disabling essential tremor of the dominant hand refractory to propranolol and primidone. She prefers a nonimplant procedure and has no cognitive impairment. Which option is most appropriate?
options: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy of the ventral intermediate nucleus
Bilateral radiofrequency pallidotomy of the globus pallidus interna
Subthalamic nucleus stimulation on both sides
Botulinum toxin injection into the hypothalamus
items.explanation: Medication-refractory essential tremor can be treated with deep brain stimulation or lesioning of the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus, and focused ultrasound offers an incisionless unilateral option. Bilateral lesions risk speech and swallowing problems and are avoided. Pallidal and subthalamic targets are used mainly for Parkinson disease and dystonia, and the hypothalamus is not a tremor target.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has asymmetric apraxia, myoclonus, and alien limb phenomena. Autopsy of such a patient most commonly shows which of the following?
options: Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra only
Corticobasal degeneration with astrocytic plaques and tau pathology
Pick bodies confined to the temporal pole
items.explanation: Corticobasal syndrome is a clinical picture, and the most frequent pathologic substrate is corticobasal degeneration, a four-repeat tauopathy with astrocytic plaques, though Alzheimer and progressive supranuclear palsy pathology can produce it. Lewy body disease would be expected to respond to levodopa, prion disease progresses within months, and Pick disease underlies behavioral or language-variant frontotemporal dementia.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a sudden onset of a coarse right arm tremor that disappears when she is distracted by a counting task and changes frequency when she taps the opposite hand to a rhythm. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Functional movement disorders show internal inconsistency, with distractibility, entrainment to an externally imposed rhythm, variable frequency, and sudden onset or remission. They represent a genuine neurologic disorder, diagnosed on positive signs rather than by exclusion. Essential and physiologic tremor have consistent frequency despite distraction. Holmes tremor follows a structural lesion and persists at rest and action. Physiotherapy-based treatment is effective.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has 3 years of unsteady gait, urinary urgency with retention, and orthostatic hypotension with a drop to 80/50 mmHg on standing. Examination shows poor levodopa response, stridor at night, and bilateral cerebellar signs. MRI would most likely show which finding?
options: Hummingbird sign of midbrain atrophy with a relatively preserved pons
Hot cross bun sign in the pons with putaminal rim atrophy
items.explanation: Early severe autonomic failure with parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia indicates multiple system atrophy, here the cerebellar type with nocturnal stridor. Characteristic imaging includes a pontine hot cross bun sign, middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy, and a putaminal slit-like rim. A hummingbird sign points to progressive supranuclear palsy, hippocampal atrophy to Alzheimer disease, and caudate atrophy to Huntington disease.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man given prochlorperazine for nausea develops painful sustained upward eye deviation and neck extension 6 hours later. Which treatment gives the fastest resolution?
options: Intravenous or intramuscular diphenhydramine or benztropine
Intravenous phenytoin loading followed by maintenance dosing
items.explanation: Acute dystonic reactions occur within hours to days after D2 blocking drugs and are more common in young men. Anticholinergic agents such as benztropine or diphenhydramine give rapid relief, often within minutes. Levodopa and phenytoin are not effective, and prolonged observation leaves a painful and frightening problem untreated. The offending agent should be stopped or replaced.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has an asymmetric stiff, clumsy left arm that does not obey her, with myoclonic jerks, cortical sensory loss, and ideomotor apraxia. Which syndrome is most likely?
items.explanation: Asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb phenomena, and focal myoclonus form the corticobasal syndrome, whose pathology is most often a four-repeat tauopathy though Alzheimer disease can also underlie it. Essential tremor lacks apraxia and sensory loss, and Parkinson disease responds to levodopa without cortical signs. Wilson disease occurs in younger patients with psychiatric and hepatic findings.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has chorea, orofacial dyskinesia with tongue and lip biting, seizures, and a distal neuropathy. Creatine kinase is elevated and a peripheral blood smear shows spiculated red cells. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Chorea-acanthocytosis is an autosomal recessive disorder due to VPS13A mutations, with chorea, prominent orolingual dystonia and self-biting, seizures, myopathy with raised creatine kinase, and acanthocytes on a smear. Huntington disease is dominant without raised creatine kinase, Sydenham chorea follows streptococcal infection in children, and Wilson disease features copper abnormalities and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Muscle biopsy is rarely needed, and treatment is supportive with attention to feeding and seizure control.

items.stem: A pharmacist explains why carbidopa is combined with levodopa in a fixed tablet for a patient with Parkinson disease. Which mechanism best explains the purpose of carbidopa?
options: Inhibition of peripheral aromatic amino acid decarboxylase
Inhibition of central monoamine oxidase B
Blockade of catechol-O-methyltransferase in the gut
items.explanation: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier and blocks dopa decarboxylase in the periphery. This reduces conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain, so more levodopa reaches the striatum while nausea and orthostatic hypotension decrease. MAO-B inhibition is the action of selegiline and rasagiline, COMT blockade is the action of entacapone, and direct D2 stimulation is the action of dopamine agonists.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of ataxia and vertigo lasting hours, triggered by stress, with interictal nystagmus. His mother has similar episodes. Which treatment is most likely to prevent attacks?
items.explanation: Episodic ataxia type 2 is an autosomal dominant calcium channelopathy from CACNA1A mutations, with attacks of hours and interictal downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus. Acetazolamide reduces attack frequency in most patients, and 4-aminopyridine is an alternative. Episodic ataxia type 1 has shorter attacks with myokymia and responds to sodium channel blockers. Levodopa, steroids, and tetrabenazine do not prevent attacks.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops a fine postural tremor of both hands, heat intolerance, weight loss, and a resting heart rate of 112. Which is the best next test?
options: Brain MRI with contrast and angiography
items.explanation: Enhanced physiologic tremor is a fine, rapid postural tremor aggravated by thyrotoxicosis, caffeine, stress, and drugs including valproate, lithium, beta-agonists, and tricyclic antidepressants. With systemic signs of hyperthyroidism, thyroid function testing is the logical test. Ceruloplasmin is for suspected Wilson disease with neuropsychiatric features, and imaging tests would add little at this stage. Treating the hyperthyroid state with antithyroid drugs and beta-blockade usually resolves the tremor within weeks.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman is placed on valproate for epilepsy and 3 months later develops a postural hand tremor, weight gain, and mild parkinsonism. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The syndrome is permanent in all patients
Valproate can cause a reversible tremor and parkinsonism
Valproate acts as a dopamine agonist
These effects are unrelated to drug exposure and reflect new neurodegeneration
items.explanation: Valproate is among the antiseizure drugs most often linked to postural tremor and to a reversible parkinsonian syndrome, which can be confused with Parkinson disease and may be accompanied by cognitive slowing. Dose reduction or discontinuation usually leads to improvement over weeks to months. Valproate does not act as a dopamine agonist. Checking ammonia and liver enzymes is also reasonable when new neurologic symptoms appear during valproate therapy.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with a vertical gaze palsy, early falls, and axial rigidity asks about treatment options. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Deep brain stimulation reliably restores gait
No disease-modifying therapy exists, and levodopa gives limited and transient benefit
items.explanation: Management of progressive supranuclear palsy is supportive, with a levodopa trial for rigidity, physical therapy for falls, speech and swallowing therapy, and botulinum toxin for blepharospasm or dystonia. No therapy has been shown to modify progression. Deep brain stimulation has not helped axial symptoms in this disorder, and immunotherapy and MAO-B inhibitors are not effective.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has 2 years of irritability, clumsiness, and fidgety movements. His father died in an institution at age 55. A genetic test confirms Huntington disease. Which finding explains his disorder?
options: An expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in HTT on chromosome 4
A CGG repeat expansion in FMR1
A GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene on chromosome 9
A CTG repeat expansion in DMPK
items.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant polyglutamine disorder caused by CAG expansion of 36 or more repeats in HTT, with full penetrance at 40 or more repeats. Anticipation occurs mainly with paternal transmission. A CGG expansion causes fragile X syndromes, a GAA expansion causes Friedreich ataxia, and a CTG expansion causes myotonic dystrophy type 1.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with Parkinson disease for 9 years has disabling motor fluctuations and dyskinesia despite optimized medication. He remains cognitively intact, has no psychiatric illness, and his symptoms respond well to levodopa. Which is the best next step?
options: Switch to a single large daily levodopa dose
Begin a cholinesterase inhibitor and observe for 6 months
Referral for deep brain stimulation evaluation
Start a trial of a typical antipsychotic
items.explanation: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna suits patients with a clear levodopa response and refractory fluctuations or dyskinesia who lack dementia or significant psychiatric disease. Large single doses worsen fluctuations. A cholinesterase inhibitor addresses cognition, not motor complications, and typical antipsychotics worsen parkinsonism through D2 blockade. Candidates are also screened for dementia, depression, and anatomical contraindications before surgery is planned.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman feels unsteady while standing still, relieved immediately by walking or sitting. Examination shows a fast 14 to 16 Hz tremor of the legs palpable on the quadriceps when standing, with a normal gait. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Orthostatic tremor is a high frequency leg tremor on standing that is often heard as a rhythmic thumping with a stethoscope or seen on surface electromyography, and it resolves on walking or sitting. Parkinson tremor is 4 to 6 Hz at rest, and cerebellar tremor is a slow intention tremor. Functional tremor shows distractibility and entrainment. Clonazepam and gabapentin are treatment options.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson disease reports dizziness on standing. Blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg supine and 94/58 mmHg after 3 minutes standing, without a rise in heart rate. He is on carbidopa-levodopa, pramipexole, and tamsulosin. What is the best initial approach?
options: Remove or reduce contributing drugs and start nonpharmacologic measures
Add a diuretic to lower supine pressure
Increase pramipexole to improve vascular tone
items.explanation: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson disease is worsened by dopaminergic agents, alpha-blockers, and antihypertensives, so the first step is to trim these and use fluids, salt, compression garments, and head-of-bed elevation. Drug therapy such as droxidopa, midodrine, or fludrocortisone follows if needed. Midodrine at bedtime would aggravate supine hypertension, and a diuretic or higher agonist dose would deepen the drop on standing.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man has 8 months of slow, magnetic gait, urinary urgency, and mild forgetfulness. CT shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Which test best predicts benefit from shunting?
options: Improvement in gait after high-volume lumbar puncture
Elevated opening pressure above 30 cm of water
Presence of the apolipoprotein E4 allele
A positive dopamine transporter scan with asymmetric uptake loss
items.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline, with ventriculomegaly beyond that expected for atrophy. A positive response to removal of about 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, or to extended lumbar drainage, predicts shunt benefit. Opening pressure is by definition normal, and neither apolipoprotein E nor dopamine transporter imaging selects shunt candidates.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a 6-month history of tremor and slowness. Which feature would most strongly argue against idiopathic Parkinson disease and prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis?
options: Presence of constipation and reduced smell
Absence of any response to adequate doses of levodopa
items.explanation: Clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson disease require bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, with supportive features including a clear levodopa response, olfactory loss, and levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Lack of response to an adequate trial suggests an atypical parkinsonian disorder. Asymmetric onset, hyposmia, constipation, and micrographia are all typical of idiopathic disease and do not weaken the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with genetically confirmed Huntington disease has troublesome chorea that interferes with eating, and she is not depressed. Which medication is approved to treat the chorea?
items.explanation: Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors, tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, and valbenazine in some regions, deplete presynaptic dopamine and reduce chorea. They carry a boxed warning for depression and suicidality, so use requires screening in a patient with Huntington disease. Levodopa and dopamine agonists can worsen chorea, and carbamazepine has no established role for it. Dose adjustment is guided by tolerability, and CYP2D6 genotype affects the maximum dose for some of these drugs.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with Parkinson disease on pramipexole is brought by his spouse because he now spends hours shopping online and has accumulated large debts. He denies a problem. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reduce or withdraw the dopamine agonist
Add a second dopamine agonist to control the urges
items.explanation: Impulse control disorders such as compulsive shopping, hypersexuality, and binge eating occur in a minority of patients on dopamine agonists, with risk higher in younger men and those with prior history. The first measure is to taper the agonist, balanced against withdrawal syndrome risk, with levodopa adjusted as needed. Raising the dose or adding another agonist would worsen the behavior, and reassurance risks serious harm.

items.stem: A 31-year-old guitarist has developed cramping and curling of two fingers of the right hand only while playing, with normal function otherwise. Strength and reflexes are normal. What is the best explanation?
options: Essential tremor of the dominant hand
items.explanation: Musician's dystonia is a task-specific focal dystonia triggered by a highly practiced skilled movement and unrelated to weakness. Writer's cramp is the classic equivalent. Motor neuron disease would produce weakness and wasting, carpal tunnel syndrome produces sensory and median motor symptoms, and essential tremor has no task-triggered finger posturing. Botulinum toxin and retraining therapies are the usual treatments.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman with dementia with Lewy bodies has excessive daytime confusion and disruptive visual hallucinations that distress her family. She is intolerant of motor decline with antipsychotics. Which first-line drug is most reasonable?
items.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors improve cognition, hallucinations, and fluctuations in dementia with Lewy bodies and are first line. Haloperidol carries severe neuroleptic sensitivity risk with potential for fatal reactions, olanzapine worsens parkinsonism, and diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and increases confusion. If an antipsychotic is unavoidable, low-dose quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin are the more tolerable choices. Rivastigmine is well tolerated, with monitoring for nausea, weight loss, bradycardia, and worsening tremor.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has progressive stiffness of the trunk and legs with painful spasms triggered by sudden noise or touch. Serum shows high titers of antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase and she has type 1 diabetes. Which is the best first-line symptomatic treatment?
items.explanation: Stiff person syndrome is an autoimmune disorder with high titer anti-GAD65 antibodies, axial and proximal limb rigidity, and startle-induced spasms. Benzodiazepines, especially diazepam or clonazepam, and baclofen are first-line symptomatic drugs, with immunotherapy such as intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. Levodopa, amantadine, and tetrabenazine do not address the GABAergic dysfunction. Electromyography shows continuous motor unit activity that is relieved by benzodiazepines, and cancer screening is advised when other antibodies are present.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with newly diagnosed neurologic Wilson disease and moderate dystonia starts therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate for initial treatment of symptomatic disease?
options: Copper supplements combined with a high-copper diet and shellfish meals
A chelator such as trientine or penicillamine, then zinc maintenance
Liver transplant immediately in all cases
items.explanation: Symptomatic Wilson disease is treated with copper chelation using trientine or D-penicillamine, which can transiently worsen neurologic symptoms with D-penicillamine, followed by zinc to block intestinal copper absorption. Dietary copper restriction supports therapy and supplements would be harmful. Transplantation is reserved for fulminant liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis not responsive to therapy. Monitoring uses 24-hour urinary copper and nonceruloplasmin-bound copper, and therapy is lifelong with attention to adherence.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman who survived a cardiac arrest 2 weeks ago develops action-induced jerks of the arms and face that worsen when she reaches for a cup. Which drug is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Post-hypoxic action myoclonus, the Lance-Adams syndrome, is a cortical myoclonus that improves with levetiracetam, valproate, or clonazepam, and piracetam where available. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate some myoclonic syndromes and do not control cortical myoclonus. Haloperidol worsens movement problems and has no role here. Symptoms often improve gradually over months, and sedating drugs should be introduced cautiously in these patients.

items.stem: A 15-year-old boy has brief episodes of dystonic and choreic posturing lasting under a minute, triggered by standing abruptly from a chair. Between episodes he is normal and his father had similar episodes in youth. Which drug is most effective?
items.explanation: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia is typically due to PRRT2 mutations and is triggered by sudden movement, with attacks lasting seconds to minutes. It responds dramatically to low-dose sodium channel blocking antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine or phenytoin. Levodopa and tetrabenazine have no consistent effect, and immunotherapy is not indicated for this inherited channelopathy. Doses far below those used for epilepsy are usually sufficient, and attacks often remit in adulthood.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa three times daily notes that each dose now lasts about 3 hours and she becomes slow and stiff before the next dose. Her pill diary shows no dyskinesia. Which change is most appropriate?
items.explanation: End-of-dose wearing off reflects a shortening levodopa response as nigrostriatal terminals are lost. Options include adding a COMT inhibitor, an MAO-B inhibitor, or a dopamine agonist, or giving levodopa more often. Entacapone extends the effect of each dose by blocking peripheral levodopa breakdown. Trihexyphenidyl does not treat fluctuations and impairs cognition, donepezil is for dementia, and an anticholinergic alone cannot replace levodopa.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with tremor and slowness undergoes dopamine transporter SPECT imaging. Which diagnosis is most likely if the scan shows normal bilateral striatal uptake?
items.explanation: Dopamine transporter imaging shows reduced striatal uptake in disorders with presynaptic nigrostriatal loss, including Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, and dementia with Lewy bodies. A normal scan supports a postsynaptic or non-degenerative cause such as drug-induced parkinsonism, essential tremor, or functional parkinsonism. The scan cannot separate the degenerative parkinsonian disorders from each other.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has slowly progressive gait ataxia with positive antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, and she has hypothyroidism. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Lifelong gluten-free diet alone without any further testing or immunotherapy
Immunotherapy trial and screening for other autoimmune disease
items.explanation: Anti-GAD cerebellar ataxia is an autoimmune cerebellar disorder often seen with other autoimmune diseases such as diabetes and thyroid disease, and it may respond partially to immunotherapy. Gluten ataxia is a separate entity diagnosed with antigliadin or transglutaminase antibodies. Chelation addresses Wilson disease, and surgery has no role. Cerebrospinal fluid often shows oligoclonal bands, and a hunt for coexisting thyroid and diabetes disease is part of care.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with Parkinson disease is started on rasagiline. His physician reviews medications to avoid dangerous interactions. Which drug combination warrants the most caution with this agent?
items.explanation: Selective MAO-B inhibitors such as rasagiline are safe with levodopa and dopamine agonists, and they are often given together. Opioids such as meperidine, along with tramadol, methadone, and dextromethorphan, can precipitate serotonin syndrome in combination with MAO inhibitors and should be avoided. Cyclic antidepressants and other serotonergic drugs also warrant caution. The tyramine concern applies mostly to nonselective MAO inhibitors, so dietary restriction is generally unnecessary at standard doses.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl develops emotional lability and irregular, semi-purposeful movements of her hands and face 4 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. Echocardiogram is normal. Which feature is typical of this disorder?
options: Progressive loss of independent ambulation within 6 months
Milkmaid grip with variable hand grip strength
items.explanation: Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever and appears weeks to months after group A streptococcal infection, with emotional lability, hypotonia, and a milkmaid grip. Carditis may coexist, so echocardiography and penicillin prophylaxis are required. Steady neurodegeneration, cherry red spots, and corneal rings point to other conditions. Treatment includes penicillin prophylaxis, and symptoms usually resolve over several months, with valproate or carbamazepine used for severe chorea.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student has deteriorating handwriting, dysarthria, tremor, and a new personality change. Examination shows golden-brown corneal rings on slit lamp. Which laboratory pattern is expected?
options: Low serum ceruloplasmin with elevated 24-hour urinary copper
High serum ceruloplasmin with low 24-hour urinary copper excretion
Normal ceruloplasmin with high serum ferritin
Low serum copper with high urinary copper
items.explanation: Wilson disease results from ATP7B mutations that impair biliary copper excretion, producing hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease with Kayser-Fleischer rings. Typical findings are low ceruloplasmin, elevated urinary copper, and elevated hepatic copper, and serum free copper is raised even though total copper is low. High ceruloplasmin or normal ceruloplasmin with ferritin elevation would not fit. Hepatic involvement is usually present, and family members should be screened because the disease is autosomal recessive.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man treated with phenytoin for 20 years has progressive gait ataxia and cerebellar atrophy on MRI, and his phenytoin levels have been supratherapeutic. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Atrophy always reverses fully within 1 week of stopping the medication
Cerebellar toxicity relates to long-term high levels and may persist
The ataxia must be a Friedreich ataxia variant
items.explanation: Chronic phenytoin exposure and especially high serum levels can cause permanent cerebellar atrophy with ataxia and nystagmus. Acute toxicity improves when levels fall, but atrophic change may persist. Other causes of acquired ataxia include lithium, chemotherapy agents such as cytarabine, and solvent exposure, and a careful drug history is part of the evaluation of any acquired ataxia.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man acts out his dreams, punching and shouting during sleep, and his wife has been struck several times. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. Which statement about his future risk is most accurate?
options: He has a high risk of developing a tauopathy such as Alzheimer disease only
He has a high risk of developing a synucleinopathy over the next decade
His risk of neurodegeneration is not higher than average
He will develop a prion disorder within months
items.explanation: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder is a prodromal synucleinopathy, and most patients eventually develop Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy. Longitudinal series show conversion rates that rise steadily over years. It is not a marker of prion disease and is not specific to tau pathology. Melatonin or clonazepam can protect against injury while safety measures are taken.

items.stem: A 12-year-old girl has disruptive motor and vocal tics that affect school performance. Education has been provided. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Haloperidol at high dose as sole first-line treatment
items.explanation: When tics are bothersome, comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics is first line because it is effective and free of drug adverse effects. Pharmacotherapy follows, starting with alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine or clonidine, then low-dose aripiprazole or other antipsychotics, or VMAT2 inhibitors. Deep brain stimulation is reserved for severe refractory adult cases, and benzodiazepines are not recommended as treatment.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has peak-dose choreiform movements of the limbs about an hour after each levodopa dose. Her off periods are manageable. Which agent is approved to reduce dyskinesia in this setting?
items.explanation: Amantadine, an NMDA receptor antagonist with other actions, reduces levodopa-induced dyskinesia and is the established option for peak-dose chorea. COMT inhibitors such as entacapone and MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline prolong dopaminergic effect and may increase dyskinesia. Benztropine is anticholinergic and does not target dyskinesia while adding cognitive and urinary side effects. Extended-release formulations are available, and adverse effects include hallucinations, leg edema, and livedo reticularis.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man with Parkinson disease for 11 years now has progressive forgetting, fluctuating attention, and visual hallucinations. Mini-Mental State Examination is 21 of 30. Which medication has the best evidence for cognitive benefit?
items.explanation: Dementia in Parkinson disease responds modestly to cholinesterase inhibitors, and rivastigmine is approved for this indication, also easing hallucinations and attentional symptoms. Memantine has limited evidence. Quetiapine treats psychosis but does not improve cognition, and trihexyphenidyl is anticholinergic and will worsen memory, confusion, and hallucinations. Nausea, tremor, and weight loss are the commonest adverse effects, and a transdermal patch can improve gastrointestinal tolerance for many patients.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman on long-term pramipexole for restless legs now reports symptoms beginning at 2 pm, spreading to the arms, and responding for shorter periods after each dose. Which is the best interpretation and plan?
options: Tolerance, so increase the agonist dose until symptoms are controlled
Augmentation, so lower the agonist and switch to a gabapentinoid
Rebound only, so add a second agonist
items.explanation: Augmentation is a paradoxical worsening of restless legs on dopaminergic therapy, with earlier daily onset, spread to other body parts, and shorter benefit from doses, and it is common on agonists and levodopa. Increasing the dose worsens it. Management is to lower or stop the agonist, ensure adequate iron, and use an alpha-2-delta ligand. Adding a second agonist continues the problem.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has declining school grades, depression, and mild dysarthria. Brain MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the putamen and thalamus. Which screening test is most appropriate?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid 14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC testing
Repeat lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
Slit lamp examination and serum ceruloplasmin
items.explanation: Wilson disease should be considered in any young patient with unexplained movement disorder, psychiatric change, or liver disease, and MRI often shows basal ganglia and thalamic signal change. Slit lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings and ceruloplasmin are the screening tests, with 24-hour urinary copper as confirmation. The prion protein assay, creatine kinase, and oligoclonal bands do not address this presentation.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor present for 10 years that interferes with eating soup with a spoon. It runs in his father's family. He has asthma and a resting heart rate of 58. Which first-line drug is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Propranolol and primidone are the first-line drugs for essential tremor, but propranolol is contraindicated in asthma and in significant bradycardia. Primidone is a reasonable alternative and is started at a very low dose to limit sedation and acute dizziness. Levodopa does not treat essential tremor, and trihexyphenidyl has weak evidence and anticholinergic effects. Clinical response should be reviewed after a few weeks because tolerance to initial dizziness usually develops.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibodies develops new generalized chorea. MRI is unremarkable. Which is the most appropriate evaluation and management?
options: Treat the underlying autoimmune disease and consider warfarin
Start tetrabenazine only and stop further evaluation and workup
items.explanation: Chorea can complicate lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome, probably through immune and thrombotic mechanisms, and treatment targets the underlying disease with immunosuppression and consideration of antithrombotic therapy such as warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant. Symptomatic VMAT2 inhibitors can be added but are not sufficient alone. Dopamine transporter imaging would not alter management. Immunosuppression with corticosteroids is commonly used, and the chorea often resolves over weeks to months.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has rigid slow movements, dystonia, and declining school performance, and his father died of Huntington disease at age 38. Which statement best explains his early presentation?
options: Maternal transmission of a small intermediate allele expansion
Paternal transmission of a very large CAG expansion in HTT
A de novo mutation in ATP7B
Autosomal recessive inheritance of an unrelated gene
items.explanation: Juvenile Huntington disease, the Westphal variant, presents before age 20 with rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonia, seizures, and cognitive decline instead of chorea, and is linked to very large CAG expansions, usually above 60 repeats, that expand further on paternal transmission through anticipation. Wilson disease is unrelated here, and a maternal small expansion would not explain the early onset.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with parkinsonism, orthostatic syncope, and erectile dysfunction has a poor levodopa response. Which feature favors multiple system atrophy over Parkinson disease?
options: Severe early autonomic failure with rapid progression
Marked and sustained improvement with a low dose of levodopa
Anosmia as an isolated early feature
items.explanation: Early prominent dysautonomia including urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension, and erectile failure, plus rapid progression, poor levodopa response, and inspiratory stridor point to multiple system atrophy. Asymmetric rest tremor, sustained levodopa benefit, and hyposmia favor Parkinson disease. Autonomic symptoms do occur in Parkinson disease, but usually later and less severely. Probable diagnosis also requires disease onset after age 30 and exclusion of other causes such as drugs or structural lesions.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa-levodopa and ropinirole. His wife reports well-formed visual hallucinations of children in the house for 3 weeks. He is oriented, and examination shows no new focal deficit. What is the most appropriate first adjustment?
options: Add haloperidol at a low dose at bedtime
Taper and stop the dopamine agonist
items.explanation: Hallucinations in treated Parkinson disease are often drug related, and the agents most likely to cause them are anticholinergics, amantadine, and dopamine agonists, so these are reduced first, after excluding infection and metabolic causes. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and risperidone worsen parkinsonism. If psychosis persists after simplifying therapy, pimavanserin, quetiapine, or clozapine can be used. Raising levodopa would likely worsen the symptom.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has delayed motor milestones, a nonprogressive generalized chorea, and recurrent lung infections. Thyroid function is abnormal and Huntington testing was normal. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Benign hereditary chorea, also called NKX2-1 related disorder, presents in early childhood with nonprogressive chorea, hypotonia, and sometimes hypothyroidism and lung disease because NKX2-1 is needed for brain, thyroid, and lung development. HTT causes Huntington disease, ATP7B causes Wilson disease, and FXN causes Friedreich ataxia. Intelligence is usually normal and the chorea often improves in adulthood.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has constipation, a pill-rolling tremor, and reduced smell. A relative asks which gene variant is the most common genetic risk factor for Parkinson disease worldwide. What is the best answer?
options: Homozygous mutations in the PINK1 gene
items.explanation: Variants in GBA1, the gene for glucocerebrosidase, are the most common genetic risk factor and carriers have earlier onset and greater cognitive risk. LRRK2 G2019S is the most common cause of monogenic dominant disease in certain populations. SNCA triplication is very rare and severe, and PINK1 and DJ-1 cause rare recessive early-onset forms. Genetic testing is not routinely required, but carriers should receive counseling about modest penetrance and about risks in relatives.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has worsening clumsiness and slurred speech. Examination shows loss of vibration sense, areflexia in the legs, Babinski signs, kyphoscoliosis, and high-arched feet, and echocardiography shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Homozygous GAA repeat expansion in FXN
CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3 on chromosome 14
items.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is the most common hereditary ataxia, an autosomal recessive disorder from GAA expansion in FXN causing frataxin deficiency, with sensory neuropathy, areflexia with extensor plantar signs, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, and diabetes. ATXN3 CAG expansion causes the dominant spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, FMR1 premutation causes fragile X tremor ataxia, and ATM mutations cause ataxia telangiectasia in younger children.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has had a gradually worsening head turn to the left with neck pain for 2 years. He relieves it by lightly touching his chin. Which is the best treatment?
options: Long-term high-dose benzodiazepine monotherapy as the sole treatment
Botulinum toxin injections into the involved neck muscles
items.explanation: Cervical dystonia causes sustained or intermittent involuntary contractions with abnormal head posture and a sensory trick, called a geste antagoniste. Botulinum toxin injected into the dystonic muscles is first-line treatment and improves both posture and pain. Benzodiazepines are less effective and limited by sedation, surgery for structural disease is not indicated, and steroids have no role. Deep brain stimulation is for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has subacute progressive gait and limb ataxia with downbeat nystagmus over 3 months. Serum anti-Yo antibodies are positive. Which next step is most important?
options: Recommend genetic testing for Friedreich ataxia and spinocerebellar ataxias
Search for an underlying gynecologic or breast malignancy
items.explanation: Subacute pancerebellar syndrome with anti-Yo (anti-PCA1) antibodies is paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, usually associated with ovarian or breast cancer. The neurologic disease often precedes tumor diagnosis, so imaging and tumor search are essential, and treatment of the tumor and immunotherapy may stabilize but rarely reverse the deficit. Hereditary ataxia would not evolve over months, and levodopa and acetazolamide do not help.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has progressive ataxia, areflexia, and retinitis pigmentosa. Serum vitamin E is undetectable and he has fat malabsorption. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Dietary protein restriction and caloric supplementation
items.explanation: Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency from TTPA mutations or from fat malabsorption produces a Friedreich-like picture with proprioceptive loss and retinopathy. High-dose vitamin E supplementation prevents progression and may improve signs, so it should be started early. Chelation treats Wilson disease, protein restriction does not apply, and baclofen treats spasticity rather than the cause. Alpha-tocopherol transfer protein defects can be confirmed genetically, and treatment is lifelong at doses well above dietary needs.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with Parkinson disease notices her afternoon levodopa doses are less effective on days she eats a high-protein lunch. Which advice is most appropriate?
options: Take levodopa 30 minutes before meals and redistribute protein to the evening meal
Take levodopa with a high-protein shake
Switch to a dopamine agonist for all doses
items.explanation: Large neutral amino acids from dietary protein compete with levodopa for intestinal absorption and transport across the blood-brain barrier, so protein can blunt doses in patients with fluctuations. Taking levodopa before meals and shifting protein to the evening helps without causing malnutrition. Permanent protein avoidance is harmful, and taking levodopa with protein worsens the problem.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a slow, large amplitude, proximal tremor of the right arm present at rest, with posture, and during movement, after a midbrain hemorrhage 3 months ago. Which term describes this tremor?
options: Essential tremor with an intention component
items.explanation: Holmes tremor is a low frequency tremor of under 4.5 Hz that is present at rest, on posture, and with action, usually due to lesions of the brainstem, thalamus, or cerebellum with an interval of weeks to months after the insult. Essential tremor is postural and kinetic without a structural cause, physiologic tremor is fine and low amplitude, and orthostatic tremor occurs only on standing.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has sudden-onset generalized myoclonic jerks and asterixis on a background of end-stage kidney failure and poor urine output. What is the best next step?
options: Start high-dose valproate immediately without any other measures or dialysis
Treat the encephalopathy with dialysis and review renally cleared drugs
items.explanation: Multifocal myoclonus with asterixis in uremia reflects metabolic encephalopathy, and treatment of the cause, including dialysis, is the priority along with review of drugs that accumulate in kidney failure, such as gabapentin, baclofen, and cefepime. Antimyoclonic drugs may be used for symptoms but cannot replace correction of the cause. Levodopa and biopsy are inappropriate. Levetiracetam dose must also be reduced for kidney impairment, and electroencephalography helps exclude nonconvulsive status.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has 3 years of intention tremor, gait ataxia, and executive dysfunction. His grandson has intellectual disability and autism. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the middle cerebellar peduncles. Which test is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Fragile X tremor ataxia syndrome affects older carriers of a premutation of 55 to 200 CGG repeats in FMR1, mainly men, with intention tremor, ataxia, and cognitive decline, and the middle cerebellar peduncle sign on MRI. A grandchild with full mutation fragile X syndrome supports the diagnosis. The other tests do not match the family history and imaging.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman develops fluctuating alertness, vivid visual hallucinations, and mild parkinsonism, and her cognitive problems precede motor signs by 2 years. After a single dose of haloperidol for agitation she becomes rigid and unresponsive. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Core features of dementia with Lewy bodies include fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism, with severe sensitivity to neuroleptics as a supportive feature. Dementia that appears at least a year before or together with motor signs defines dementia with Lewy bodies, whereas dementia arising well after established Parkinson disease is labeled Parkinson disease dementia. Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia lack this combination.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early falls has sagittal brain MRI performed. Which finding is characteristic?
options: Pontine hot cross bun sign with cerebellar peduncle atrophy
Midbrain atrophy giving a hummingbird appearance
items.explanation: Midbrain tegmental atrophy with preserved pons produces the hummingbird or penguin silhouette on sagittal images and the morning glory sign on axial images in progressive supranuclear palsy. Hot cross bun change suggests multiple system atrophy, caudate atrophy suggests Huntington disease, and cortical ribboning on diffusion imaging suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Slowed vertical saccades appear first, and downward gaze is typically lost before upward gaze, aiding bedside recognition.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman treated with metoclopramide for gastroparesis develops symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity within 3 months. Which statement best describes the management?
options: Withdraw the offending drug, and expect improvement over weeks to months
Begin high-dose levodopa while continuing the drug
items.explanation: Drug-induced parkinsonism from D2 blockers such as metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and antipsychotics is typically symmetric and usually improves after stopping the agent, though recovery can take months and some patients unmask underlying Parkinson disease. Continuing the drug while giving levodopa is illogical, and haloperidol would worsen the picture. A presynaptic dopamine transporter scan is normal in pure drug-induced cases.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with multiple system atrophy has supine blood pressure of 170/100 mmHg and symptomatic drops on standing to 80/50 mmHg. Which approach is most appropriate for his hypotension?
options: Raise the head of the bed, avoid lying flat in daytime, and use short-acting agents such as droxidopa carefully
items.explanation: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with supine hypertension is common in synucleinopathies. Management uses head-up sleeping, compression, salt and fluid, and short-acting pressors such as droxidopa or midodrine in the daytime, avoiding doses close to bedtime. Long-acting nighttime pressors or diuretics worsen one of the two problems, and beta-blockers lower pressure without addressing standing hypotension. Patients should also avoid large meals, hot environments, and sudden standing, and may benefit from abdominal binders.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has restless legs symptoms every evening that disturb sleep. Ferritin is 28 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is normal. Which is the most appropriate step?
options: Start a high-dose dopamine agonist as first line and titrate upward
Iron replacement and an alpha-2-delta ligand such as pregabalin
Order polysomnography to confirm the diagnosis
items.explanation: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, and ferritin at or below about 75 ng/mL is an indication for iron therapy. Current guidance favors alpha-2-delta ligands over dopamine agonists as first-line drugs because agonists carry a risk of augmentation, with earlier and worse symptoms. Opioids are a last resort, and polysomnography is not needed to make the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for years. After a bout of vomiting and dehydration he develops coarse tremor, gait ataxia, and dysarthria. What is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Lithium commonly causes a postural tremor and, with elevated levels from dehydration, kidney impairment, or interacting drugs such as thiazides and NSAIDs, produces ataxia, dysarthria, and confusion, with a risk of lasting cerebellar damage. Management is hydration, stopping the drug, and dialysis in severe cases. Wilson and Huntington disease do not follow an acute exposure pattern, and Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with Huntington disease reports persistent low mood, hopelessness, and early morning awakening. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Start an antidepressant such as an SSRI and assess suicide risk
Attribute the symptoms to normal disease progression and simply observe
items.explanation: Depression is frequent in Huntington disease and suicide risk is elevated, so mood symptoms warrant active treatment, usually with SSRIs and psychotherapy, plus a safety assessment. VMAT2 inhibitors can cause or worsen depression and should be reduced or stopped when mood worsens. Observation alone is unsafe, and haloperidol alone does not treat depression. Suicidal ideation is a medical emergency in this population and demands immediate assessment and specialist referral when present.
